title: UIS-Digger: Towards Comprehensive Research Agent Systems for Real-world Unindexed Information Seeking
one_liner: Build a research agent that does not stop at search results but also opens hard-to-reach pages and files that search engines miss.
lead: Many research agents look strong on benchmarks because the needed facts are already indexed by search engines. Real work is messier. Important facts may sit behind dynamic page elements, inside attached files, or on pages that crawlers never captured well. This paper names that gap unindexed information seeking and shows that current agents fail badly on it. UIS-Digger addresses the gap with a multi-agent system that can browse pages and parse files at the same time. That matters because a search result alone may only point toward the answer, while the answer itself lives inside a report, spreadsheet, or expanding page section.

problem.h2: Why search-only agents miss real evidence
paras: A modern search agent usually starts by sending a query to a search engine, opening the top links, and summarizing what it sees. That works when the answer is visible in indexed page text. It fails when the answer is hidden in places the index did not capture: a file download, a table revealed after a click, or content loaded only after a page script runs.

The failure is easy to underestimate because common benchmarks reward agents for reaching public facts that are already easy to index. In practice, analysts, researchers, and journalists often need the messy remainder. They need the appendix file, the missing attachment, the page section below a tab control, or the updated number inside an embedded document.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Treat page browsing and file extraction as parallel first-class actions, because the answer may be split across both.

steps.text: The agent starts from a search hit or seed page that may contain or point to the answer.
One branch clicks, expands, and scrolls through the page to reveal content that plain indexing missed.
A second branch downloads and reads attached files such as reports or tables.
The branches exchange evidence so the system can decide whether a lead is worth pursuing.
The final answer is produced from the merged page and file evidence.

paras: The paper changes the action space of a research agent. Instead of treating web search as the main path and file handling as an afterthought, it makes page interaction and file parsing equal parts of the same workflow.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: evidence coverage beyond the index
hidden.name: How much of the answer space the agent can actually reach
paras: The key quantity is not only answer accuracy. It is evidence coverage: how much of the relevant material the agent can access at all. An agent may reason well and still fail because it never reaches the file or page element where the answer lives.

UIS-Digger measures this gap by constructing questions whose answers sit in unindexed places and comparing systems on that set. Large drops on the new benchmark show that standard search-centered agents lose access before reasoning even begins. The dual-mode design aims to close that gap by increasing the fraction of reachable evidence.

heat.caption: Darker means the answer path depends on material beyond ordinary indexed text.

reads.html: The important question is whether the agent can even get to the evidence, because reasoning cannot recover facts the agent never reached.
UIS-QA isolates questions whose support lies in unindexed content such as dynamic pages and attached files, so evaluation exposes evidence-reach failures directly.

mechanism.h2: Why dual-mode browsing recovers hidden answers
paras: The method works because it removes a false assumption built into many agents: that page text visible to a search engine is close to the full evidence set. In UIS tasks that assumption breaks. A search result may only provide the doorway. The decisive number may be inside a downloadable document or behind a page control that must be opened.

UIS-Digger assigns separate branches to these two evidence types so neither blocks the other. While one branch explores the live page, the other can read the attached file and extract structured facts. The branches share their findings, which lets the system connect clues across formats. This improves final accuracy because the missing fact often appears only when page context and file content are joined together.

stages.s: Candidate page from a search result
Merge page facts and file facts
Answer supported by evidence beyond the index

math.words: Measure accuracy on tasks whose evidence lies in unindexed sources and compare it with accuracy on ordinary indexed benchmarks.
symbols: accuracy on benchmarks where search-engine indexed content is usually enough
accuracy on tasks where evidence lies in dynamic pages or attached files
the performance drop caused by missing unindexed evidence

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an agent answers 71 of 100 indexed benchmark questions correctly.
Now test it on 100 questions where the answer sits in dynamic content or attached files.
It answers only 25 of those correctly.
A smaller gap means the agent is better at reaching and using hidden evidence.

math.note: The gap matters because a strong indexed score can hide a severe failure on real evidence that search engines do not expose directly.

charts.title: Ordinary indexed evaluation
charts.note: Indexed benchmarks still reward strong search and reading behavior.

charts.title: UIS evaluation
charts.note: UIS-Digger wins on the new setting because it is designed to reach page and file evidence that standard agents skip.

items.b: The agent opens the wrong files.
items.html: A page may link many attachments, and only one matters. If the file branch chases noisy files, time and budget are wasted before the useful evidence is found.

Some pages require login, scripted navigation, or repeated interaction. The dual-mode design helps, but it cannot recover material that the agent is not allowed to access because no page browser or file parser can read content that the system is blocked from opening.

items.b: Evidence from page and file conflicts.
items.html: A live page may be newer than a linked document, or a file may contain a draft value. The system must compare timestamps and source roles because simply merging all text can produce a wrong answer.

When page exploration and file parsing run together and their evidence is reconciled carefully, the agent answers more real questions because it can reach the hidden support that search-only systems leave behind.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark of fifty questions where the answer sits partly in visible page text and partly in an attachment or collapsed page section. Compare a search-only agent against a dual-mode agent that can browse and parse files in parallel. The demo should show a clear drop for the search-only system and a smaller drop for the dual-mode system because reaching the hidden evidence is the real barrier.
demo.closing: The visible lesson should be that better reasoning is not enough when the answer source itself is out of reach, because the agent cannot infer facts from evidence it never accessed.
